Consult Summary:
- 31-year-old man with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, sore, red, cracked skin on chest, hands and antecubital areas; clinician impression: eczema flare — plan for topical steroid, emollient, and possible oral antihistamine with review in 1 week.

History:
- Presenting complaint: widespread itchy, sore, red skin for approximately four days, described as very itchy and disruptive to sleep and work.
- Distribution/onset/duration/progression: started 3–4 days ago; mainly chest, hands, inside elbows/arms; more extensive and itchier than his prior eczema (prior eczema mainly on arms).
- Associated symptoms: skin cracking in places; no bleeding, pus, fever, cough, breathing difficulties; bowel and urine normal.
- Pertinent negatives: no facial involvement; no systemic symptoms reported.
- Past medical history: prior eczema; past asthma (stated "not anymore").
- Medications: no regular medications. Recent self-purchased "steroid cream" from pharmacy — dose/route/frequency not documented. Patient reports recent use of antihistamines which he states did not help — name/dose/frequency not documented. Previously prescribed topical cream and a shower/bath product for eczema in the past — names/doses not documented.
- Allergies: patient reports no known allergies.
- Social history / preventive care: age ~31, lives with flatmates, works full-time (project manager at a pharmaceutical company), occasional alcohol, non-smoker.

Examination:
- Vitals: none documented.
- Examination findings: none objectively documented. (Clinician stated the rash "appears familiar" but no specific examination findings recorded.)

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: likely eczema flare (atopic dermatitis exacerbation).

Plan:
- Topical therapy: clinician to prescribe a stronger topical corticosteroid (specific agent/dose/route/frequency to be prescribed; not documented in transcript).
- Emollients: prescribe/use emollient for bath/shower and regular skin moisturization; advised use for first 7–10 days.
- Oral antihistamine: suggested trial of an oral antihistamine; clinician offered Fexofenadine as an option (to be prescribed) — patient has trialed OTC antihistamines previously without benefit.
- Self-management/advice: keep a diary of potential triggers (soaps, shower gels, clothing); avoid identified triggers if found.
- Follow-up: return or re-contact clinician in about one week if symptoms do not improve.
- Tests/referrals: none ordered or mentioned.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but expected elements: vital signs, objective skin examination details (description of rash morphology), specific medication names/doses/routes/frequencies for prescribed topical steroid, emollient, and any oral antihistamine; medication reconciliation details for OTC products used; severity assessment and safety-netting detail (e.g., signs of infection to seek urgent care) not documented.
- Internal conflicts: timing of onset reported as "a few days/three days" and also specifically "four days" (conflict noted). Clinician states he would examine the rash but no documented exam findings; clinician also stated "having looked at your skin" though no examination details provided (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: audio intermittently poor with brief inaudible segments; substance of consult overall coherent but some sections unclear.
